newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe firms spurn cellphone project offer.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe firms spurn cellphone project offer.

text.p: Two black-led Zimbabwean firms spurned on Wednesday a government offer that they join winners of a controversial tender to set up the country's first private cellular telephone service.

SupaNet and Tritell Cellular said in a statement equity participation in winners Telecel Zimbabwe's project as announced by Information, Posts and Telecommuncations Minister Joyce Mujuru a fortnight ago did not make commercial sense.

"Further, our review of the winning bid has raised fundamental questions on the adjudication process that will require consultations with our legal counsel before making our position on the tender process public," the statement said.
"Based on the above, we would like to place it on record that we will not form an alliance with Telecel Zimbabwe," it said.

According to the official Herald newspaper, Christopher Mutsvangwa of Tritel alleged that Telecel's bid failed to comply with the tender requirements in key aspects, describing its financial bid as "meaningless".
"The business plan is commercially plunderous to Zimbabwe and extortionate to minority stakeholders," he told the Herald.

When she announced winners of the tender on March 6, Mujuru said Telecel -- a joint venture between a Zairean-based firm and a consortium of black Zimbabwean businesses and pressure groups -- should accommodate the four losing bidders to the tune of 15-20 percent equity in the operating entity.

One of the losers, Econet -- which has been involved in lengthy court battles to get a licence -- immediately said it would not be involved in the Telecel project, saying it was an operator in its own right.
Econet alleged in a statement that the tender process was rigged in favour of Telecel.
Mujuru and government tender board chairman Stanley Mahlahla stoutly deny any irregularities in the tender procedure.
